title: What a valid will needs and what makes one fail
summary: A will is valid only if the person making it had the mental capacity to make it, made it freely, and signed it in the form the law requires. Most failed wills fail on one of those three tests, or because the original cannot be found.
body:
Bottom line. A will must pass three tests: the person had capacity, the person acted freely, and the will was signed in the required form. Fail any one and the will may be set aside, so that the law, not you, decides who inherits. Keep the original safe, because a missing original is its own kind of failure.

In plain English

A will is a written document that says who receives your property when you die and who manages your estate. The person who makes a will is the testator. If you die without a valid will, you die intestate, and a statute sets out who inherits. In Alberta, both wills and intestacy are governed by the Wills and Succession Act (Alberta).

Courts protect a will that is properly made. They also protect families from wills that were not truly the testator's own. So the law sets tests. They are not technicalities. Each one answers a real question: did this person understand, did they choose freely, and is this really their document?

The framework

  1. Capacity. Testamentary capacity means the testator understood what a will is, knew roughly what they owned, knew who would normally expect to benefit, and understood the effect of the will. A medical diagnosis does not automatically remove capacity, and capacity can vary from day to day.
  2. Free will. The will must reflect the testator's own choice. Undue influence is pressure strong enough to override that choice. A will made by someone who was pressured, or tricked, can be set aside.
  3. Knowledge and approval. The testator must have known and approved what the will says. This matters when someone else drafted it, especially a person who benefits.
  4. Formal requirements. In Alberta, a formal will is generally in writing, signed at the end by the testator in the presence of two witnesses who are present at the same time, and signed by those witnesses [unverified — confirm independently]. Alberta also generally recognizes a holograph will, which is a will wholly in the testator's own handwriting and signed by them, without witnesses [unverified — confirm independently].
  5. Witness conflicts. A gift to a witness, or to a witness's spouse or partner, can be void even when the rest of the will stands [unverified — confirm independently]. Use witnesses who receive nothing.
  6. Revocation. A will can be revoked by a later will, by deliberate destruction, or in some cases by a change in relationship status, such as divorce affecting gifts to a former spouse [unverified — confirm independently].
  7. The original. Courts generally need the original. If the testator kept it and it cannot be found, the law may presume they destroyed it on purpose [unverified — confirm independently].

Alberta courts also have a power to accept some documents that do not meet every formal rule, if there is clear evidence the document reflects the testator's intention [unverified — confirm independently]. Do not plan to rely on it. It is a rescue, not a method.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. All numbers are round and invented for teaching.

A developer with an estate of about 3,000,000 types a new will himself on a laptop. He prints it, signs it at the bottom, and asks his assistant and his nephew to witness it. The nephew is left 100,000. The assistant signs that afternoon; the nephew signs the next day.

Three problems. First, the witnesses were not present together when he signed [unverified — confirm independently]. Second, the nephew witnessed a will that benefits him, so his gift may fail [unverified — confirm independently]. Third, the will is typed, so it cannot be a holograph will. His family now faces a court application to decide whether the document counts. If it fails, an earlier will, or the intestacy rules, may decide the estate.

A lawyer-supervised signing would have cost a small fraction of the court process, and would have produced a record of his capacity on the day.

Professional Sign-Off Required: wills and estates lawyer.

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is to think a signature is enough. Witnessing rules are strict, and getting them slightly wrong can cost a family years.

The second mistake is to make or change a will while ill, under stress, or with a beneficiary in the room. Even if the will is valid, those facts invite a challenge. If your health is uncertain, ask the lawyer to make a note of your capacity, or to get a short medical opinion at the time of signing.

How you will use it

Have every will signed in a lawyer's office, with two independent witnesses who receive nothing. Ask the lawyer to keep the original in their vault and give you a copy marked as a copy. Tell your executor where the original is. Keep notes, in your own words, of why you made unusual choices, such as leaving more to one child. Those notes are useful evidence if anyone later says you did not understand or did not choose freely.

Each time you sign a new will, confirm with the lawyer which earlier wills it revokes and that the earlier originals are dealt with.
checklist: Confirm the will is in writing and signed at the end.
Use two independent witnesses, present together, who receive nothing.
Sign when you are well, with no beneficiary in the room.
Ask the lawyer to record evidence of capacity if your health is uncertain.
Keep the original in a lawyer's vault and tell your executor where it is.
Write a short note explaining any unusual choices.
Confirm which earlier wills each new will revokes.

selftest.q: Your brother, who is named as a beneficiary, offers to witness your will at your kitchen table, and a neighbour will sign as the second witness the next morning. What is wrong with this?
selftest.a: Two problems. A witness who is a beneficiary, or a beneficiary's spouse, can lose their gift. And the formal rules generally require both witnesses to be present together when you sign. The will may be challenged or partly fail. Sign in a lawyer's office with two independent witnesses present at the same time.

apply: Find out where the original of your current will is, and write down who witnessed it and whether either receives anything under it.
sources: Wills and Succession Act (Alberta) is named as the Alberta statute for wills and intestacy. The formal signing rules, holograph wills, witness-beneficiary rules, revocation on divorce, the presumption about a missing original, and the court's power to validate non-compliant documents are all tagged [unverified — confirm independently]; confirm against the current consolidated statute from the Alberta King's Printer. Capacity elements are described conceptually. Figures hypothetical. Education only; not legal advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: wills and estates lawyer.

title: Executors, guardians, specific vs residual gifts
summary: Your will chooses an executor to run your estate, can name a guardian for young children, and divides property through specific gifts and a residue. How you write the gifts decides who bears the loss when assets change, so choose people carefully and draft gifts that still work if your assets are different at death.
body:
Bottom line. The two biggest decisions in a will are who runs it and how the property is divided. Choose an executor for ability and a guardian for your children's care. Write most of your estate as a residue shared by percentage, because specific gifts can fail or swallow the estate when your assets change.

In plain English

An executor is the person you name to manage your estate after death. In Alberta the general term is personal representative [unverified — confirm independently]. The executor collects assets, pays debts and taxes, files the final tax returns, deals with the court if probate is needed, and distributes what is left. It is a real job, often lasting a year or more.

A guardian is the person who will care for your children under the age of majority. You can name a guardian in your will, but a court can decide differently if that serves the child's best interests [unverified — confirm independently]. A guardian cares for the child. Managing money left for the child is often a separate role, given to a trustee.

Gifts in a will come in two broad kinds. A specific gift is a named item or amount: "my car to my brother," "100,000 to my niece," "my shares of a named company to my son." The residue, or residuary gift, is everything left after debts, taxes, expenses and specific gifts are paid.

The framework

  1. Choose an executor for ability. They need honesty, organization and time. For a business owner, consider whether they can work with your accountant, lawyer and partners. Name at least one alternate. Consider a professional or trust company as co-executor for a complex estate.
  2. Give the executor real powers. The will can expressly allow them to run or sell a business, hold or sell land, borrow and invest. Without clear powers, the executor may need court approval.
  3. Choose a guardian for care, and a trustee for money. They can be the same person or different people. Name alternates.
  4. Write specific gifts sparingly. Keep them for items with personal meaning or a clear reason.
  5. Know what happens when assets change. If a specific item is no longer owned at death, the gift usually fails. Lawyers call this ademption. If the estate is too small to pay everything, gifts are reduced in an order set by law, called abatement, and the residue is usually reduced first [unverified — confirm independently].
  6. Know what happens when a beneficiary dies first. A gift to a person who dies before you may fail, called lapse, unless the will or the law redirects it [unverified — confirm independently]. Say in the will who takes instead.
  7. Make the residue the main gift. Divide it by percentages, which adjust automatically as values change.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. All numbers are round and invented for teaching.

A developer's will leaves "my shares of Project Company A to my son," "500,000 cash to my daughter," and "the residue to my wife." When he writes it, his estate is 3,000,000: the shares are worth 1,000,000.

Five years later, Project Company A is wound up and its value moved into Project Company B. He dies with an estate of 1,200,000, mostly in Company B shares. His son's specific gift fails, because he no longer owns Company A shares. His daughter's 500,000 is paid. After tax and expenses, his wife's residue is only about 400,000.

The will reversed his intentions. A better draft would leave the residue in percentages to all three, with any specific gifts kept small and described so they survive a restructuring.

Professional Sign-Off Required: wills and estates lawyer; chartered professional accountant (CPA) for the tax and estate figures.

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is to describe company shares by the name of a company that will change, or a fixed cash amount from a plan that assumes today's values. Developers restructure often. A will that names entities goes stale with every reorganization.

The second mistake is to name the eldest child as executor out of custom, without asking whether they have the time or skill, or whether it will cause conflict with siblings.

How you will use it

Before your next will meeting, write a short brief. List your executor, alternate, guardian and trustee, and one sentence on why each was chosen. List any specific gifts and ask your lawyer: "What happens to this gift if I restructure, sell, or lose value?" Ask that the residue be expressed in percentages. Then ask your executor, in person, whether they will accept the job, and give them a list of your advisers.

After every restructuring, sale or large purchase, ask one more question: does any gift in my will name an asset or company that just changed? If yes, the will needs a review, even if nothing else in your life has changed. A short letter from your lawyer confirming the will still works is cheap. A failed gift is not.
checklist: Choose an executor and an alternate for ability, not custom.
Give the executor express powers to run or sell a business and deal with land.
Name a guardian for care and, if different, a trustee for money, with alternates.
Keep specific gifts few and describe them so they survive a restructuring.
Divide the residue by percentages.
State who takes a gift if a beneficiary dies before you.
Ask each person named whether they will accept the role.

selftest.q: Your will leaves "my rental condo on Main Street to my daughter" and the residue to your son. You sell the condo and put the cash into a new project. You die two years later. What happens?
selftest.a: The specific gift likely fails by ademption because you no longer own the condo, so the sale proceeds fall into the residue and go to your son. Your daughter may receive nothing, which reverses your intention. Use percentages of the residue, or describe gifts so they survive a sale, and update the will after major transactions. A wills and estates lawyer must review.

apply: Write down your executor, alternate, guardian and trustee, and one sentence on why you chose each.
sources: Concept lesson. The term personal representative, a court's power on guardianship, the order of abatement and the rules on lapse are tagged [unverified — confirm independently] and are governed in Alberta by the Wills and Succession Act (Alberta) and related legislation; confirm against current statutes. Figures hypothetical. Education only; not legal advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: wills and estates lawyer; chartered professional accountant (CPA).

title: Wills and trusts together: testamentary and spousal trusts, minors
summary: A will can create trusts that start at death, so property is held and managed for a spouse, minor children or others instead of being handed over outright. A testamentary trust can protect young or vulnerable beneficiaries, and a properly drafted spousal trust can defer tax while controlling where the capital ends up.
body:
Bottom line. Leaving property outright is simple, but it gives up control the moment the gift is made. A trust in your will lets you decide how and when property reaches each person. It protects minors, can support a spouse while preserving capital for your children, and can carry tax advantages when it meets the rules.

In plain English

An earlier topic explained a trust: a settlor gives property to a trustee, who holds and manages it for beneficiaries under written terms. A trust made while you are alive is an inter vivos trust. A trust created by your will, which starts at your death, is a testamentary trust.

Why use one? Because an outright gift ends your control. A 19-year-old can spend an inheritance in a year. A surviving spouse who remarries may leave everything to a new partner. A beneficiary with a disability may lose government benefits if they receive a lump sum [unverified — confirm independently]. A trust lets you set the rules in advance.

Minors are a special case. A child under the age of majority, 18 in Alberta [unverified — confirm independently], generally cannot receive and manage an inheritance directly. Without a trust in the will, money for a minor may have to be paid to a government trustee office or held under court supervision until the child is an adult [unverified — confirm independently], and then paid out all at once.

The framework

  1. Decide who needs a trust. Minors, young adults, people with disabilities, beneficiaries with creditor or relationship risk, and a surviving spouse when you want to protect capital for children.
  2. Choose the trustee. Often the executor, sometimes with a co-trustee for balance. Name alternates.
  3. Set the distribution rules. For children, a common pattern is income and capital for education and support, then capital in stages at chosen ages, such as a third at each of three ages.
  4. Consider a spousal trust. Under section 70(6) of the Income Tax Act (Canada), property left to a trust can pass at its tax cost, deferring the deemed disposition, if the trust meets the conditions. In general, the spouse or common-law partner must be entitled to all the income during their lifetime, and nobody else may receive or use the capital while they live. The capital then passes to whoever the will names, such as the children.
  5. Check the tax position of each trust. An estate may qualify as a graduated rate estate, defined in section 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (Canada), for a limited time [unverified — confirm independently]. Trusts also face the 21-year deemed disposition under section 104(4) of the Act.
  6. Coordinate with family claims. In Alberta, certain family members, including a spouse and dependent children, may be able to apply to court for support from an estate if the will does not adequately provide for them [unverified — confirm independently]. A trust should be designed with that in mind.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. All numbers are round and invented for teaching.

A developer, in a second marriage, has two children from his first marriage, aged 12 and 16. His estate is about 4,000,000, including private company shares with a large untaxed gain.

A simple will leaving everything to his wife would defer the tax under the spousal rollover, but his wife could later leave all of it to anyone. Leaving everything to the children would trigger the full tax at his death and give teenagers large sums.

His lawyer proposes a spousal trust holding the company shares. His wife receives all the income for life, and nobody else may receive capital while she lives, so the gain is deferred. At her death, the capital passes to his children. Separately, a trust for each child holds 500,000 of insurance proceeds, used for education and support, with capital paid at three staged ages.

His wife is supported. His children's inheritance is protected. The tax is deferred and partly funded.

Professional Sign-Off Required: wills and estates lawyer; tax lawyer and chartered professional accountant (CPA).

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is to add one extra power to a spousal trust, such as letting the trustee pay capital to a child during the spouse's life. That can disqualify the trust from the spousal rollover, so the full tax falls due at the first death [unverified — confirm independently].

The second mistake is to leave money to a minor outright. The result is court or government supervision and a full payout at 18, which is the opposite of what most parents intend.

How you will use it

For each beneficiary, write one line: outright, or in trust, and why. For each trust, write the trustee, the purpose, and the ages or events at which capital is paid. Ask your tax adviser to confirm in writing that any spousal trust meets the rollover conditions as drafted. Review these trusts whenever a child reaches a milestone or a relationship changes.
checklist: Decide for each beneficiary: outright or in trust, and why.
Never leave a minor an outright gift.
Name a trustee and alternates for each testamentary trust.
Set staged ages or events for paying capital.
Confirm a spousal trust gives the spouse all income and nobody else capital during the spouse's life.
Ask about family maintenance claims before finalizing.
Have a tax adviser confirm the rollover conditions in writing.

selftest.q: You want your second spouse supported for life but want your company shares to end up with your children, and you want to defer the tax at your death. What structure fits, and what drafting trap must you avoid?
selftest.a: A testamentary spousal trust: the spouse gets all the income for life, nobody else may receive or use capital during the spouse's life, and the capital passes to the children at the spouse's death. This can defer the deemed disposition under section 70(6). The trap is adding powers, such as capital payments to children during the spouse's life, which can disqualify the trust. A wills and estates lawyer, tax lawyer and CPA must sign off.

apply: List each person in your will and write next to their name whether they should inherit outright or through a trust.
sources: Income Tax Act (Canada): section 70(6) (transfer to spouse or spousal trust), the definition of graduated rate estate in section 248(1), and section 104(4) (21-year deemed disposition), cited by name; confirm current text and conditions with a CPA. The age of majority in Alberta, payment of a minor's inheritance to a government trustee, effects on disability benefits, family maintenance claims under Alberta law, and disqualification of a spousal trust are tagged [unverified — confirm independently]. Figures hypothetical. Education only; not legal or tax advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: wills and estates lawyer; tax lawyer and chartered professional accountant (CPA).

title: The review cycle: updates, cross-border wills, final checklist
summary: An estate plan goes stale as your family, assets, companies and countries change, so it needs a review on a set schedule and after specific events. If you own property in more than one country, you may need wills that work together, and the documents across your whole plan must agree.
body:
Bottom line. An estate plan is a living set of documents, not a one-time event. Review it on a schedule and after every major change. If you have assets in more than one country, make sure each country's documents work with the others, because a careless new will can cancel the old one.

In plain English

This is the last lesson of the course. It ties the estate topics together and turns them into a habit.

A will is written for the facts on the day it is signed. Those facts change. You form companies, sell land, marry, separate, have grandchildren, move countries. Laws change too. A will that was right ten years ago can now give the wrong result, as earlier lessons showed with failed specific gifts and stale beneficiary designations.

Cross-border property adds a layer. Each country has its own rules about what makes a will valid, which law applies, and what process the executor must follow. As a general concept in common law systems, land is usually governed by the law of the place where it sits, while other property is usually governed by the law of the place where the deceased was domiciled, meaning their permanent home [unverified — confirm independently]. Someone with property in Canada and Guyana, for example, needs to think about both systems, and Guyana's rules should be confirmed with a lawyer qualified there [unverified — confirm independently].

The framework

  1. Set a schedule. A full review every three to five years, and a quick check every year.
  2. Know the trigger events. Marriage, separation, divorce, a birth or death in the family, a new company or restructuring, a large purchase or sale, a move to a new province or country, a serious illness, and a change in the person you named as executor, attorney or guardian.
  3. Review all documents together. Will, enduring power of attorney, personal directive, beneficiary designations, joint titles, shareholder agreements, trust deeds and insurance. They must agree with each other.
  4. For cross-border assets, coordinate wills. Some people use separate wills for property in different countries. Each must say which assets it covers, and the revocation clause in each must not cancel the others [unverified — confirm independently]. A standard clause revoking "all prior wills" can wipe out a foreign will by accident.
  5. Check executors can act where the assets are. Some places restrict non-resident executors or require extra steps or security [unverified — confirm independently].
  6. Keep an estate binder. One place listing documents, originals' locations, advisers, accounts, companies, and guidance on where passwords are kept, so your executor can start without searching.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. All numbers are round and invented for teaching.

A developer living in Alberta owns Canadian companies worth about 5,000,000 and a family property in Guyana worth about 300,000. Years ago he made a will in Guyana covering the property there, and later a Canadian will.

At a review, his lawyer notices the Canadian will begins: "I revoke all former wills." That clause may have revoked the Guyana will. If so, the Guyana property may pass under the Canadian will or under the rules for intestacy, and the executor may face an unfamiliar court process [unverified — confirm independently].

The fix: a new Canadian will limited to his property outside Guyana, expressly preserving the Guyana will, and a check by a lawyer qualified in Guyana that the Guyana will is still valid and suitable. His accountant also reviews whether either country taxes the property at his death [unverified — confirm independently].

Professional Sign-Off Required: wills and estates lawyer in Alberta; lawyer qualified in Guyana; chartered professional accountant (CPA) for cross-border tax.

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is to sign a new will in one country without telling the lawyer about property or wills elsewhere. Lawyers draft for the facts they are given.

The second mistake is to treat the review as a reading exercise. A review only counts if it ends in a decision: no change needed, or a list of changes with a date.

A third mistake is to forget the people. Executors, attorneys, guardians and trustees age, move, fall ill and fall out with each other. A plan that names the right people from ten years ago may name the wrong people today.

How you will use it

Put two dates in your calendar: a yearly quick check and a full review every few years. Use the checklist that goes with this lesson each time. Bring your one-page estate map from lesson 49, your totals table from lesson 52, and your control map from lesson 44 to the meeting. Arriving with those means your lawyer spends the time on judgment rather than on gathering facts, which is the habit this whole course has been building. Thinking like a lawyer, in the end, means knowing the question, the rule, and the facts before you pay someone to answer.
checklist: Set a yearly quick check and a full review every three to five years.
Review after any trigger event: family, assets, companies, moves, illness.
Review the will, powers of attorney, directive, designations, titles and agreements together.
For each country, confirm which will covers which assets and that revocation clauses do not conflict.
Confirm your executor can act where your assets are.
Keep an estate binder listing documents, originals and advisers.
End every review with a written decision and a date.

selftest.q: You have a will in Guyana for a house there and are about to sign a new Alberta will prepared from a standard template. What must you raise with your Alberta lawyer?
selftest.a: Tell the lawyer about the Guyana house and the Guyana will. A standard clause revoking all former wills could cancel the Guyana will. The Alberta will should be limited to property outside Guyana and expressly preserve the Guyana will, and a lawyer qualified in Guyana should confirm the Guyana will is still valid. Ask a CPA about tax in both countries.

apply: Put a yearly estate-plan check in your calendar and list every document and every country where you own property.
sources: Concept lesson. The conflict-of-laws principle for land and other property, Guyana's will and succession rules, the effect of revocation clauses on foreign wills, restrictions on non-resident executors, and tax at death in either country are all tagged [unverified — confirm independently]; confirm with a lawyer qualified in each jurisdiction. Figures hypothetical. Education only; not legal or tax advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: wills and estates lawyer in Alberta; lawyer qualified in Guyana; chartered professional accountant (CPA).
